deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (prev. page, Krafft): Euler wants all primes 4n±1 for which ±a is a quadratic residue (QR). His key fact: if the prime is 4ap+i^2 (i odd), then ±a are residues. Put i=2c+1. Then 4n+1=4ap+(2c+1)^2 gives n=ap+c(c+1). Reduce c(c+1)=0,2,6,12,20,... mod a. Call the residues obtained r and the other classes rho. Four theorems follow. I: 4n+1 prime, n≡r mod a gives ±a QR and a^{2n}≡1. II: n≡rho gives ±a non-residues and a^{2n}≡-1. III: 4n-1 prime, n≡-r gives +a QR, -a not, and a^{2n-1}≡1. IV: n≡-rho gives -a QR and a^{2n-1}≡-1. This page works the examples.

2) a=3. c(c+1) mod 3 gives r={0,2}, rho={1}.
- I: n=3p or 3p+2 gives 4n+1=12p+1 or 12p+9. The latter is divisible by 3 and is rejected. So for p≡1 (mod 12), x^2±3y^2 and 3^{2n}-1 are divisible.
- II: n=3p+1 gives 12p+5, and 3^{2n}+1 is divisible.
- III: n=3p-0 or 3p-2 gives 4n-1=12p-1 (12p-9 drops out). For p≡11 (mod 12), x^2-3y^2 and 3^{2n-1}-1 are divisible.
- IV: n=3p-1 gives 12p-5≡7 (mod 12), and x^2+3y^2 and 3^{2n-1}+1 are divisible.

3) a=5. c(c+1) mod 5 = 0,2,1,2,0,... so r={0,1,2}, rho={3,4}≡{-2,-1}.
- I: 4n+1=20p+1, (20p+5 rejected), 20p+9.
- II: 20p-3, 20p-7.
- III: 4n-1=20p-1, (20p-5), 20p-9.
- IV: 20p+3, 20p+7.
In modern terms: 5 is a QR exactly when p≡±1 (mod 5).

4) a=6. c(c+1) mod 6 gives r={0,2}, rho={1,3,4,5}.
- I: 24p+1 (24p+9 rejected).
- II: n=6p+1, 3, -2, -1 gives 24p+5, 13, -7 (24p-3 is divisible by 3).
- III: 24p-1 (24p-9 rejected).
- IV: n=6p-1, -3, +2 gives 24p-5, -13, +7.

Euler then flags an error. Rho=1 should belong to r, so 24p+5 belongs in case I. Check: for n=0 the divisor is 5, and 6≡1 is a residue mod 5. By the same token, 24p-5 (≡19 mod 24) belongs in III rather than IV. Euler leaves this implicit under 'idem inconveniens'.

The printed text says the trouble arises whenever 'n' is even; a is meant. Euler's ad hoc remedy for even a: c(c+1)=2T with T triangular, and he reduces T modulo a/2.
- For a=6, T mod 3 ∈ {0,1}, which adds 1 to r.
- For a=10, c(c+1) mod 10 gives {0,2,6}. T mod 5 gives {0,1,3}, so r={0,1,2,3,6} and rho={4,5,7,8,9}.
- Then 4r+1 = 1, (5), 9, 13, (25) and 4rho+1 = 17, 21, 29, 33, 37 ≡ 17, -19, -11, -7, -3 (mod 40).
- Euler says 9 must also move from rho to r, i.e. 37 belongs with the residues. Correct: the classes p≡1 (mod 4) with (10/p)=1 are {1,9,13,37} mod 40.

LEXELL'S NOTE. The real cause is compositeness of a. If a is prime, the r/rho lists are right. If a is composite, the r found are right but incomplete. For the prime 2x+1, (ab)^x≡1 can arise in two ways.
- (i) a^x≡1 and b^x≡1: then (ab)^x-b^x=b^x(a^x-1)≡0; add b^x-1. The rule supplies these cases.
- (ii) a^x≡-1 and b^x≡-1: then (ab)^x+b^x≡0; subtract b^x+1, leaving (ab)^x-1≡0. These are the cases wrongly put under rho.
This is multiplicativity of the quadratic character via Euler's criterion: non-residue times non-residue is a residue.

REFORMULATION. Let 2m+1 be prime. If 2m+1=4ab+i^2, then ±a are residues. If 2m+1=4ab-i^2, only +a is. In either case a^m≡1 (mod 2m+1). Euler says the proof is not yet complete. The next page attempts it: from 4ab+i^2, -ab and hence ab is a residue, and he tries to split off the factors.
errors: Example a=6: assigning rho=1 (n=6p+1) to case II puts primes 24p+5 among those for which 6 is a non-residue. In fact (6/p)=(2/p)(3/p)=(-1)(-1)=+1 for p≡5 mod 24. Euler himself detects and corrects this.

Example a=6, case IV: n=6p-1 gives 4n-1=24p-5≡19 (mod 24). For such p, (6/p)=(-1)(-1)=+1, so they belong in case III, not IV. This is the same defect, acknowledged only implicitly ('idem inconveniens').
Text says the inconvenience occurs 'quoties n est numerus par'. The argument (dividing c(c+1) by 2 and reducing mod a/2) shows a is meant, not n.

The triangular-number remedy for even a is heuristic, not a correct general rule. For a=10 it adds r=1 (useless, since 4n+1 then has the factor 5) and r=3 (correct, giving 13). It misses r=9 (37 mod 40), which Euler must add separately.

The general rule (p=4ab±i^2 gives a residue) is only a sufficient condition when a is composite; for prime a it gives the full set. Euler states the condition, not its proof (as he himself admits). Lexell's explanation correctly identifies the missing product-of-two-non-residues classes.

results.what: Classification of primes p for which ±3, ±5, ±6 are quadratic residues, by residue class: p≡±1 (mod 12) for 3; p≡±1 (mod 5) for 5; and the 4n±1 split determining ±a.
results.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity / supplementary laws: special cases (3/p), (5/p), (6/p), (10/p)
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat/Euler (special cases); general law conjectured by Euler (1744-1783), Legendre, proved by Gauss 1796/1801

results.what: Rule: prime p=4an+i^2 implies ±a are QR; p=4an-i^2 implies +a is QR (equivalently a^{(p-1)/2}≡1). Explored via residues of c(c+1) mod a.
results.modern_name: Euler's formulation of quadratic reciprocity (residue classes mod 4a)

results.what: Observation (Lexell's note) that for composite a=bc, (ab)^x≡1 also when a^x≡b^x≡-1. Hence the classes from odd squares mod 4a do not exhaust the primes having a as residue.
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol (via Euler's criterion); the subgroup of squares in (Z/4a)* has index >2 when a is composite

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-documented empirical work on quadratic reciprocity in the Adversaria, published in the Opera Postuma (1862). The worked examples and the composite-modulus correction (via Lexell) are mildly interesting editorial detail, but the content is known and attributed to Euler.

checkable.asserts: r-values for a=6 from c(c+1) are only 0,2 (the source of the incompleteness)

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(6, p) == 1 for p in primerange(5, 5000) if p % 24 == 5)
checkable.asserts: 6 is a QR for primes p≡5 (mod 24), so rho=1 must be moved to r (Euler's correction)

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(6, p) == 1 for p in primerange(5, 5000) if p % 24 == 19)
checkable.asserts: 6 is a QR for p≡19≡24p-5, so case IV entry n=6p-1 is misplaced (belongs to III)

checkable.sympy: all((legendre_symbol(6, p) == -1) for p in primerange(5, 5000) if p % 24 in (13, 17))
checkable.asserts: Euler's remaining case II classes 24p+13, 24p-7 are correct

checkable.sympy: sorted(set(p % 40 for p in primerange(7, 20000) if p % 4 == 1 and legendre_symbol(10, p) == 1)) == [1, 9, 13, 37]
checkable.asserts: For a=10 the residue classes are 1,9,13,37 mod 40, i.e. r={0,2,3,9} (plus excluded 1,6): 9 belongs to r as Euler states
Triangular numbers mod 5 give 0,1,3, the extra r-values Euler adds for a=10

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(5, p) == (1 if p % 5 in (1, 4) else -1) for p in primerange(7, 5000))
all(legendre_symbol(3, p) == (1 if p % 12 in (1, 11) else -1) for p in primerange(5, 5000))
all(all(legendre_symbol(d, p) == 1 for d in divisors((p - i**2)//4)) for p in primerange(5, 3000) if p % 4 == 1 for i in range(1, isqrt(p) + 1, 2) if p - i**2 > 0)
checkable.asserts: Euler's reformulation: if p=4ab+i^2, every divisor a of (p-i^2)/4 is a QR mod p

transcription_corrections: Case III for a=3: should read n=3p-0, -2 (per Theorem III, n=ap-r), consistent with 4n-1=12p-1, 12p-9.
Case III for a=6: '4n-1=24p-1, 9' should be '24p-1, -9' (the -9 class is rejected as divisible by 3).
'quoties n est numerus par' is as printed, but the sense requires 'a' (even a).
